redFlag.r1_d: Almost all your answers are on the right side: this person is decent to the people serving them, apologises when they're wrong, hears a no, and you feel safe with them. That doesn't guarantee a perfect story, nobody can promise that. But what the test looks for, the signs that keep coming back and do damage, it didn't find.
redFlag.r1_a: Keep this test in a corner of your mind: if something changes in a few months, you'll know where to find it. And if you took it because a small voice had doubts, listen to what that voice is saying exactly, because it clearly isn't about a red flag. Maybe it's about pace, or about feelings, and those are other questions.
redFlag.r2_d: A few answers pull a little: a heavy joke, a jealousy said with a laugh, a mood that rises fast and comes back down. Everyone has that, and it isn't what makes a red flag. A red flag is a behaviour that keeps coming back and hurts you, and there isn't one in your answers.
redFlag.r2_a: Nothing in particular to do, apart from staying alert to one thing: the reaction when you say what bothers you. Someone who hears a remark and changes a little is healthy. If one day that stops being the case, the test will still be here.
redFlag.r3_d: Two or three answers deserve a pause, without alarming anyone: a way of talking about exes, a conversation that revolves a lot around him or her, lateness that keeps happening, digs that come a bit too often. Taken one by one, these are ordinary flaws. What matters is that they don't add up over time.
redFlag.r3_a: Take the answer that made you wince the most when you read it, and say it, simply, the next time it happens: "when you do that, it bothers me". The reaction will tell you a lot. If it's a good one, you're dealing with someone imperfect, which is to say someone normal.
redFlag.r4_d: This time there is something. Not a disaster, but one or two behaviours that keep coming back and aren't trifles: apologies that never come, a jealousy that is starting to decide for you, people close to you being criticised, hot and cold that leaves you without bearings. You had probably noticed. The test confirms it.
redFlag.r4_a: Don't excuse it wholesale ("that's just how he is") and don't dramatise it either. Name the precise behaviour, once, calmly, and watch what happens in the weeks that follow. A change that lasts is a good sign. A change that holds for three days, or anger because you dared to bring it up, is your answer.
redFlag.r5_t: Several red flags, and they go together
redFlag.r5_d: Your answers draw a pattern, not isolated incidents: control, jealousy, anger, apologies that don't come, people close to you being pushed away. Each one alone would be debatable. Together, they say this relationship is already costing you something, and it's often your peace of mind that goes first.
redFlag.r5_a: Talk to someone who isn't part of the story, a friend you trust, and read them your answers as they are. From the inside, you play everything down; from the outside, things are visible. And ask yourself one question only: do you feel better or worse than before this relationship?
redFlag.r6_d: There's no more doubt about the direction: this person doesn't respect your limits, or keeps you on your guard, or puts you down, and often all three. It's no longer about flaws, it's a way of treating you, and it won't fix itself because you become more patient or more understanding.
redFlag.r6_a: If this is a recent encounter, you have your answer, and it saves you months. If you're already a couple, put words on it with someone outside the relationship, and give yourself a short deadline: what needs to change, and by when. Without a clear change, what comes next is you fading out, little by little.
redFlag.r7_d: Your answers describe control and fear, not a difficult relationship: watching your phone, deciding what you can do or who you can see, exploding over nothing, never admitting to being wrong, pulling you away from the people close to you. When you answer like this, you've often already started adapting to avoid the outbursts. That's exactly the sign not to ignore.
redFlag.r7_a: It isn't your job to fix this person, and it isn't your patience that's lacking. Talk to someone you trust this week, keep the people close to you close, and don't stay alone with this. If you're hesitating about what comes next, reread your answers to the questions about no and about fear: that's your compass.
redFlag.r8_d: Almost all your answers point the same way, and it's the wrong one: you're afraid of their reaction, you can't say no, you check what they tell you, the people close to you are worried and you see them less. This isn't a person with flaws, it's a relationship that is damaging you, and the test has only one level above this one.
redFlag.r8_a: Assume it won't get better by staying. Get close to someone safe right now, and if you live together, quietly get ready to leave: documents, a little money, somewhere to go. You're allowed to be afraid, and you're allowed to ask for help.
redFlag.r9_t: This isn't a red flag any more, it's a danger
redFlag.r9_d: At least one of your answers describes violence or real fear: a raised hand, hitting "for a laugh", someone who doesn't let go when you say no, or that fear of their reaction that makes you watch everything you do. No test can measure that, and no explanation, no "they're not usually like this", changes what it means: you are not safe.
redFlag.r9_a: Don't stay alone with this today. In the UK, the National Domestic Abuse Helpline (0808 2000 247) answers for free, 24 hours a day; in the US, the National Domestic Violence Hotline is 1-800-799-7233. In immediate danger, call 999 or 911. Tell someone you trust what you're living, even if you haven't decided anything yet. What you feel is not an exaggeration.
